Brevity of Life
BREV-i-tee uhv LYF
noun
The shortness of human life; from the Latin brevitas, shortness; the biblical theme of man’s fleeting days.

Biblical Definition

The brevity of life is the constant biblical theme of the shortness of man’s days—a vapor, a shadow, a handbreadth—set over against the eternity of God, and pressed upon the soul to teach it wisdom. What is your life? asks James; it is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. The psalmist measures the span: the days of our years are threescore years and ten, and if by strength fourscore, yet is their strength labour and sorrow, for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. He prays to know his end and the measure of his days, that he may know how frail he is. This is no morbid brooding but the path to wisdom: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. To reckon life short is to weigh rightly the things of time and eternity—to loosen the grip on the perishing, to redeem the fleeting hours, to set the affections on the world that does not pass away, and to make ready to meet God. The dictionary reads the brevity of life as a sober and salutary truth: man’s days are few and swift, a vapor soon gone, and the wise man, instead of living as though life were long, numbers his short days, lays up treasure in heaven, and prepares his soul for the eternity that follows the handbreadth of his years.

Webster 1828 Definition

The shortness of human life—a vapor, a shadow, a handbreadth—set against the eternity of God, pressed upon the soul to teach it to number its days unto wisdom.

Jas 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Psa 90:12 — "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

Psa 90:10 — "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."

Psa 39:4 — "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am."

Modern Corruption

The age hides death and dreams of indefinitely extended life, refusing to number its days; Scripture presses the brevity of life upon the soul to teach it wisdom and to make it ready for eternity.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the modern flight from the brevity of life. The age hides death behind hospital walls, fills the days with distraction, and dreams of indefinitely extending the span by medicine and technology, refusing to reckon that man’s days are a vapor soon gone. So men live as though life were long—hoarding, postponing, neglecting the soul—and are overtaken unready, like the rich fool whose barns were full the night his soul was required. To refuse to number one’s days is not to lengthen them but to waste them.

The principle to recover is the numbering of our short days unto wisdom. Scripture presses the brevity of life not to drive the soul to despair but to wake it to wisdom: what is your life? a vapor; our days are threescore and ten, soon cut off; so teach us to number them. The man who reckons his life a handbreadth holds the perishing loosely, redeems the fleeting time, sets his affection on the eternal world, and makes ready to meet his God. The shortness of life, rightly weighed, is a mercy that turns the heart from the dust to the things that abide for ever.
